It was very widely played throughout Hungary until the 1940s and itself gave rise to further variants. Because of its association with the gentry, it was discouraged and nearly disappeared during the Soviet occupation of Hungary. Since 1990, it has gradually gained popularity again. The game is played by 4 players forming two partnerships of 2. An advanced system of bids and bonuses gives it a strategic complexity comparable to bridge. However, unlike bridge, partnerships vary from hand to hand, determined by the card called by the high bidder. This leads to more random short-term variability in the results - but in the long run, the more skilled player always wins! Out of the various rule variants, this implementation follows the standard set of rules proposed by Lóránt Kégl. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary The rules of the game are described in detail on the ultimate resource for card games, pagat.com . Where multiple rule variants exist, this implementation uses the standard rules suggested on Lóránt Kégl's Tarokk page . Below is a summary of standard conventions and basic gameplay advice broken down according to the various phases of the game. Contents 1 Bidding 1.1 Yielded game 1.2 Invitations 1.3 Catch situations 2 Exchange 2.1 Priorities 2.2 When to keep suits we could get rid of 3 Announcements 4 Playing the hand Bidding Yielded game A: 3, B: 2, A: pass => A holds the XX (rule) and has 5+ trumps (convention) Invitations With the XIX: A: 3, B: 1, A: Hold (or Solo), B: Pass => B is making the invitation. If A plays right after B, i.e. A has the first lead, Solo should be preferred to Hold to ensure B gets 2 cards from the kitty. If a third player bids Solo after B, A can (and should) hold to accept the invitation. In this case the invitation is still successful, the third bidder intervenes only to ensure more cards for the opposing side at A’s expense. The rules allow A to pass and let the third bidder accept the invitation instead, but there are no circumstances in which this is a good idea. A: 2, B: 1 (or Solo), A: Pass => A is making the invitation. The same considerations apply: B should bid solo when playing right after A; if a third player bids, B can hold (after A has passed) and the invitation is still successful. With the XVIII: A: 3, B: Solo, A: Hold => Invitation made by B and accepted by A. A: 1, B: Solo, A: Pass => Invitation made by A and accepted by B. A: 3, B: 2, A: 1, B: Solo => Same result as in the previous case, thus usually better to go for this option (if nobody else bids, A gets 3 cards, not one). To make an invitation, a strong hand is required: 6+ trumps, a good suit (K + another), high trumps alongside the honour and the inviting card. The latter requirement can be relaxed slightly with 7 trumps or moderately with 8 or 9. If the first player to bid needs less than 3 cards from the kitty and/or wants to play a more valuable game, they have the right to bid two or one (or even solo) right away even if they do not hold the card required for an invitation. However, if another player attempts to accept what seems like an invitation, they then must bid on (usually by holding) to cancel it. When bidding with the pagat only, a stronger hand is required (6+ trumps, including 2 or 3 high). The only exception is bidding two right after three: this is safe to do even with a weak hand and makes it harder for the two high honours to get together by means of a yielded game or an invitation. It also ensures we get two cards from the kitty (possibly even by the game being yielded to us). When holding the XX and the pagat but no high honour, it is almost always a bad idea to bid, except when two others have bid already (to try to get away from the player holding the XXI in case the catch is on). Hungarian Tarokk, also known as Húszashívásos tarokk (XX-calling tarokk), or Paskievics tarokk, is a four player, variable partnership, trick taking tarot game. As with most games in this genre, the base objective of each round is to capture a certain amount of card points (in this case, more than half) in tricks. However, each round of Hungarian Tarokk starts with a peculiar round of auctions and announcements that impart a lot of information about the players' hands, which make it a very skillful, challenging, yet surprisingly accessible game.

It uses a shortened pack of 42 cards: the trump suit consists of 22 cards while the other four suits consist of only five cards each. The size of each player’s hand is only nine cards (with a talon of six cards).

Each round starts with a short auction in which players bid for the right to choose a partner that holds a particular high ranking trump card, usually the XX. The bid itself determines the number of cards the winner of the auction may exchange (higher bids mean less cards exchanged) and the base value of  game (to capture more than half of the card points in tricks) in points.

Players have restrictions on how they may bid; in particular, a player may only bid only if he or she holds an honour (the lowest trump, the second-highest trump, or the highest trump). In addition, there are bidding conventions that, unlike Bridge, are part of the rules. These conventions, or "invitation bids," indicate if a player holds a particular high ranking trump.

After players exchange cards with the talon, there is a round of announcements. Partnerships can pursue additional objectives other than game:

- Winning three-fourths of the card points
- Winning all the tricks
- Winning all three honours
- Winning all four kings
- Winning the last trick with the lowest trump
- XXI-catch: Capturing the opponent's second highest trump with the highest trump

During the round of announcements, a partnership may announce that they will accomplish one or more of these objectives, which doubles their value. A partnership may also challenge or kontra an announcement, which also doubles its value. These objectives are scored independently; a team can fail at accomplishing game but still accomplish (and score for) other objectives. Often, the value of these objectives is greater than game. For example, the base value of game ranges from 1 to 4 points, while the value of XXI-catch is 21 points.

[Rating: 5/10] BGA.  Makes some sense and can see the appeal for players, however isn't necessarily for me

[Rating: 5.5/10] I really did not understand this game at all. The rules seem to assume you know a lot of advanced trick-taking terms and conventions. The game is played counter-clockwise, there is an extra face card (the rider), then there is bidding, declaring, announcements (announcing is different than declaring?), calling a partner (yoo hoo), the talon, bonuses, contra-bonuses. My Hungarian grandmother might understand all this, but I don't.

[Rating: 6/10] I really do love tarock games but Slovenian tarock is so much better.  Only played online.

[Rating: 6.5/10] [thing=101723][/thing] is very much in the same vein as others Tarot games: you have someone making a bet (from 3 to 0, which is how many cards extra they will get), then the caller claims a partner, followed by players being able to make further bets and announce certain types of cards, for extra points.  Everything works well enough, and I found it to be less swingy than French Tarot, with less cards is more predictable, and the amount of points isn't so variable.  As with many traditional card games like this, [thing=101723][/thing] gets better with experience, and will demand many games - 

[Rating: 8/10] My friend created a player aid which really helped. The bidding is strange but the secret partner aspect and bonus points for completing certain tasks are excellent mechanics and bring a sense of anticipation and excitement to the game. One of the better trick taking games I have played (and I have played quite a few). The strange sounding rules may put off a lot of players.
